title: Solomon
summary: Solomon’s place in the biblical story connects David’s royal promise with the building of the Jerusalem temple. First Kings describes the temple’s construction during Solomon’s reign, then interrupts the building account with a reminder that God’s presence among Israel is tied to the people’s faithfulness. The passage therefore presents the temple as more than a royal achievement: it is bound to the covenant life of the community.
historical_context: The cited passages place Solomon in the royal line established through David and narrate the construction of the temple in Jerusalem. First Kings dates the project within its account to the fourth year of Solomon’s reign; that is the book’s internal chronology, not an external date independently established by the sources in this profile.
canonical_context: Second Samuel 7 frames the promise to David’s royal house, and 1 Kings 6 shows Solomon building the temple in Jerusalem. Psalm 2 contributes royal language to the profile’s wider network, but it does not name Solomon, so these anchors do not establish that the psalm was composed for his accession.
literary_context: First Kings 6 pauses its detailed account of the temple’s construction for a direct word to Solomon. The interruption shifts attention from measurements and building work to the condition for God’s presence among Israel: the king and people must keep God’s commands. That placement prevents the temple from being read as a guarantee of security simply because the building is complete.
covenantal_significance: In 1 Kings 6:12–13, God’s promise to dwell among Israel is joined to the condition that Solomon and the people walk in the commands given to them. The covenantal point is that a temple does not replace faithful life; the royal building project remains accountable to the relationship it is meant to serve.
canonical_role: The selected passages connect Solomon to David’s royal promise and to the construction of the Jerusalem temple. First Kings uses the building account to place covenant faithfulness alongside royal achievement, while Psalm 2 supplies related royal language without naming Solomon.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not flatten monarchy into simple success or failure; the narratives often hold both together.
Royal stories are always read against covenant accountability.
